## Working with Factors, Pt. 1

[Forcats cheat sheet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/factors.pdf)

```{r Load Packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(here)
library(beepr)
library(peRReo)
library(gm) # See https://flujoo.github.io/gm/ for setup
```

```{r Load Data}
# Read Directly from GitHub
income_mean <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-02-09/income_mean.csv")

head(income_mean)

# Built-in Data in {dplyr}
starwars

head(starwars)
```

### What is a factor?

- A factor is specialized version of a character
  - Value a factor can take are **levels**
  - Levels let you control the **order** of categories in plots and summaries
  - The default order of levels is always alphabetical
  - R stores factors as **integers** (1,2,3...) mapped to level labels

```{r Factor Examples}
fruits <- factor(c("Apple", "Grape", "Banana"))
fruits

# [1] Apple  Grape  Banana
# Levels: Apple Banana Grape
```

#### Reading in Data Safely

- `read.csv` = base R
  - Strings become **factors** automatically
- `read_csv` = tidyverse
  - Strings stay as **characters**
- Always use `read_csv` from {readr}

### The{forcats} Package

- **For cat**egorical data
- All main functions start with `fct_`

#### `fct_lump()` — Lump Rare Levels Together

- `fct_lump(x, n)` keeps the `n` most common levels and collapses everything else into `"Other"`
  - Result is a **factor** and no longer alphabetical, order determined by factors levels

```{r Star Wars Data}

starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |> # Remove NAs
  count(species, sort = TRUE)

star_counts <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  mutate(species = fct_lump(species, n = 3)) |>
  count(species)

star_counts
```

#### `fct_reorder()` — Sort by Another Variable

- `fct_reorder(f, x) reorders the levels of factor`f`by the values of`x\`

```{r Star Wars Bar Plot}

# Sorting is Unclear
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

# Sort by Another Variable
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Species")

# Descending Order
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n)) + # Add .desc = TRUE to flip the order
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Species")
```

```{r Income Mean Data}
total_income <- income_mean |>
  group_by(year, income_quintile) |>
  summarise(income_dollars_sum = sum(income_dollars),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    income_quintile = factor(income_quintile))

# Line Plot — Legend in Wrong Order
total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = income_quintile)) +
  geom_line()

# Reorder by Two Variables
total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = fct_reorder2(income_quintile, year, income_dollars_sum))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(color = "Income Quintile")
```

- `mutate(income_quintile = factor(income_quintile))` converts the character column to a factor so we can reorder it
- `fct_reorder2(f, x, y)` — Reorders by 2 Variables:
  - Reorders `f` by the values of `y` at the largest values of `x`
  - Aligns legend with the right end of the lines

#### Setting Levels Manually

- Use the `levels` argument inside `factor()` to set the exact order you want
  - This is especially useful for months, treatments, etc. with a meaniningful inherent order that isn't alphabetical

```{r Manual Levels}
# Without levels — alphabetical by default
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))

x1

# [1] Jan Mar Apr Dec
# Levels: Apr Dec Jan Mar

# With levels — your specified order
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"),
             levels = c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))
x1

# [1] Jan Mar Apr Dec
# Levels: Jan Mar Apr Dec
```

#### Subsetting Factors

- Filter to Common Species

```{r Filtered Star Wars}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |> # convert to factor
  filter(n > 3) # keep only common species

starwars_clean

levels(starwars_clean$species) # check the factor levels
```

#### `droplevels()` — Remove Unused Levels

- `droplevels()` (base R) or `fct_drop()` (forcats) removes any levels that no longer appear in the data

```{r Drop Levels}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels() # Removes unused levels

levels(starwars_clean$species)
# [1] "Droid" "Human"
```

#### `fct_recode` — Rename Levels

- `fct_recode(f "new name" = "old name")` renames one or more levels

```{r Rename Levels}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels() |>
  mutate(species = fct_recode(species, "Humanoid" = "Human"))

starwars_clean
```

#### Other Helpful {forcats} Functions

1.  `fct_relevel()` = Move specific levels to the front
2.  `fct_rev()` = Reverse order of levels
3.  `fct_collapse()` = Collapse multiple levels into one
4.  `fct_na_value_to_level()` = Convert NA into an explicit level
5.  `fct_infreq()` = Order levels by frequency

More reading:

- [R Factors](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/factors.html)
- [Stat 545 Factors](https://stat545.com/factors-boss.html)

## Working with Strings, Pt. 2

```{r Load Packages, Pt. 2}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(wordcloud)
library(janeaustenr)
```

### Intro to {stringr}

- What is a string?
  - A string and a character are the same thing
  - Presence of quotation indicates a string
- 4 basic families of the `stringer` package:

1.  Manipulation: functions that let you manipulate individual characters within the strings in character vectors
2.  Whitespace tools to add, remove, and manipulate whitespace
3.  Locale sensitive operations whose behavior will vary from locale to locale
4.  Pattern matching functions: recognize 4 engines of pattern description. The most common is regular expressions, but there are three other tools.

#### Manipulation

- Paste words together
  - Can be useful if you have two columns of treatments and want to combine into one

```{r Manipulation}
paste("High temp", "Low pH")

# [1] "High temp Low pH"

## Add a dash between words

paste("High temp", "Low pH", sep = "-")

# [1] "High temp-Low pH"

## Remove the space between the words

paste0("High temp", "Low pH")

# [1] "High tempLow pH"

## Working with vectors
shapes <- c("Square", "Circle", "Triangle")
paste("My favorite shape is a", shapes)

# [1] "My favorite shape is a Square"  
# [2] "My favorite shape is a Circle"  
# [3] "My favorite shape is a Triangle"
```

```{r Manipulation, Individual Characters}
## Vector of Shapes

shapes

str_length(shapes) # how many letters are in each word?

seq_data <- c("ATCCCGTC")

str_sub(seq_data, start = 2, end = 4) # extract the 2nd to the 4th amino acid

## Modifying Strings

str_sub(seq_data, start = 3, end = 3) <- "A"
seq_data

# [1] "ATACCGTC"

## Duplicating strings

str_dup(seq_data, times = c(2, 3))
# [1] "ATACCGTCATACCGTC"        
# [2] "ATACCGTCATACCGTCATACCGTC"
```

#### Whitespace

- If you have a column that has extra spaces, R will treat them as different values
- `str_trim()` can handle the messy data

```{r Removing Whitespace}
badtreatments <- c("High", " High", "High ", "Low", "Low")

badtreatments

# [1] "High"  " High" "High " "Low"   "Low" 

## Remove whitespace:
str_trim(badtreatments) # this removes both

# [1] "High" "High" "High" "Low"  "Low" 

## Want to remove only from one side?

str_trim(badtreatments, side = "left") # this removes left

# [1] "High"  "High"  "High " "Low"   "Low"
```

- Opposite of `str_trim()` is `str_pad()` to add white space to either side

```{r Adding Whitespace}
str_pad(badtreatments, 5, side = "right") # add a white space to the right side after the 5th character

# Want to add a character instead?
str_pad(badtreatments, 5, side = "right", pad = "1") # add a 1 to the right side after the 5th character
```

#### Locale Sensitive

- `str_to_upper()` makes everything upper case
- `str_to_lower()` makes everything lower case
- `str_to_title()` makes it a title case

### Pattern Matching

- {stringr} has functions to view, detect, locate, extract, match, replace, and split strings based on specific patterns
  - `str_detect()`
  - `str_view()`
  - `str_locate()`

### regex: Regular Expressions

- Here is a [cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/regex.pdf) for `regex`
- Several types of regular expressions
  - Metacharacters
    - .  \| ( ) \[ { \$ \* + ?
  - Sequences
  - Quantifiers
  - Character classes
  - POSIX character classes (Portable Operating System Interface)

#### Metacharacters

- `str_replace()` only replaces the first instance, `str_replace_all()` replaces all values

```{r Metacharacters}
vals <- c("a.b", "b.c", "c.d")

# string, pattern, replace
str_replace(vals, "\\.", " ")

# [1] "a b" "b c" "c d"
```

#### Sequences

- Sequences, as the name suggests, refer to the sequences of characters which can match

```{r Sequences}
# Subset the vector to only keep strings with digits
val2 <- c("test 123", "test 456", "test")

str_subset(val2, "\\d")

# [1] "test 123" "test 456"
```

#### Character Class

- Character class is a list of characters enclose by `[]`
- The regex character class, `[aA]`, matches any lowercase letter `a` or any uppercase `A`

```{r Character Class}
val2 <- c("test 123", "test 456", "test")

# Count number of lowercase vowels
str_count(val2, "[aeiou]")
# [1] 1 1 1

# Count any digit
str_count(val2, "[0-9]")
# [1] 3 3 0
```

#### Quantifiers

- `^` = beginning of string
- `$` = end of string
- `\n` = new line
- `+` = one or more of previous
- `*` = zero of more of previous
- `?` = zero or one of previous
- `{5}` = exactly five of previous
- `{2, 5}` = between 2 and 5 of previous
- `{2, }` = more than 2 of previous

```{r Example: Find Phone Numbers}
strings <- c("550-153-7578",
             "banana",
             "435.114.7586",
             "home: 672-442-6739")

phone <- "([2-9][0-9]{2})[- .]([0-9]{3})[- .]([0-9]{4})"

# Which strings contain phone numbers?
str_detect(strings, phone)

# [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

# Create phone number subset:
test <- str_subset(strings, phone)
test

# [1] "550-153-7578"       "435.114.7586"      
# [3] "home: 672-442-673
```

## {tidytext}

- Package for text mining and making text tidy. This is very helpful for social sciences or anyone that uses survey data
- Also really helpful for text mining abstracts to write a review paper on a topic

```{r Jane Austen Data}
# Quick Look
head(austen_books())

# Clean, add column for line and chapter
original_books <- austen_books() |> # get all of Jane Austen's books
  group_by(book) |>
  mutate(line = row_number(), # find every line
         chapter = cumsum(str_detect(text, regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]", # count the chapters (starts with the word chapter followed by a digit or roman numeral)
                                                 ignore_case = TRUE)))) |> # ignore lower or uppercase
  ungroup() # ungroup it so we have a dataframe again

# don't try to view the entire thing... it's >73000 lines...
head(original_books)

# Want only one word per row for further mining?
tidy_books <- original_books |>
  unnest_tokens(output = word, input = text) # add a column named word, with the input as the text column

head(tidy_books) # there are now >725,000 rows. Don't view the entire thing!

# Meaningless words can be removed as well!
# Example of all the stopwords
head(get_stopwords())

cleaned_books <- tidy_books |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords()) # dataframe without the stopwords

head(cleaned_books)

# What are the most common words?
cleaned_books |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)
```
